title: Down 20%, up 20% — back to even?
topic: A raise that doesn't actually undo a cut
blurb: They cut your pay 20%, then 'made it right' with a 20% raise. The AI says you're whole again.
prompt: You asked an AI to check your offer letter. Tap the line that sounds too sure of itself.

segments.label: The old salary
segments.text: Your salary was $100,000 a year before the downturn.

segments.label: The cut
segments.text: Last year the company cut your pay by 20%.

segments.label: The raise
segments.text: This year's offer gives you a 20% raise on your current salary.

segments.label: The punchline
segments.text: A 20% cut and a 20% raise cancel out, so the new offer puts you right back at $100,000.

segments.label: The closer
segments.text: You can sign today: the raise fully restores your original pay.

conclusion: AI verdict: Down 20% then up 20% returns you exactly to $100,000. Take the offer.

flaws.original: The 20% raise is applied to the reduced $80,000 salary ($80,000 × 1.20 = $96,000), so you're still $4,000 short of $100,000.
flaws.corrupted: A 20% cut and a 20% raise cancel out, so the new offer puts you right back at $100,000.

diagnosis_choices.label: The raise is 20% of the smaller $80,000 paycheck (+$16,000), which does not undo a 20% cut of $100,000 (−$20,000).
You have to adjust both years for inflation before comparing the two salaries.
20% of $100,000 is $25,000, so the cut actually landed at $75,000.
A 20% cut then a 20% raise overshoots, landing above $100,000 at $104,000.

fix_choices.label: Do it in order: $100,000 × 0.80 = $80,000, then $80,000 × 1.20 = $96,000. You'd need a 25% raise to get back to $100,000.
Average the two percentages: (20% + 20%) / 2, which keeps the salary at $100,000.
Apply both changes to the original $100,000 and add them, for a final salary of $100,000.
Keep $100,000 because multiplying by 0.80 and then 1.20 can be done in either order.

flaws.explanation: Percentages multiply, they don't cancel. A 20% cut drops $100,000 to $80,000; a 20% raise on $80,000 only adds $16,000, landing at $96,000. You need a 25% raise to recover from a 20% cut.
flaws.why_tempting: Saying '−20% + 20% = 0' feels obviously right, because we treat percentages like dollar amounts.
flaws.catch_rule: Never add sequential percentage changes; multiply the factors (0.80 × 1.20 = 0.96).
flaws.hint: What's your actual salary after the cut? Now take 20% of that new number, not of $100,000.

practice.problem: A stock you bragged about dropped 50% this month. What gain do you need next month just to get back to even?
practice.answer: A 100% gain — it has to double from the bottom.

clean_segments: Your salary was $100,000 a year before the downturn.
Last year the company cut your pay by 20%, to $80,000.
This year's offer gives you a 20% raise on that current salary.
Because 20% of $80,000 is $16,000, the new offer is $96,000 — still $4,000 short of $100,000.
Sign only if you're fine being 4% below your old pay; a 25% raise would be needed to restore it.
clean_conclusion: Down 20% then up 20% leaves you at $96,000, not $100,000.
